newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. labour chief looks to global "social label".
newsitem.headline: U.N. labour chief looks to global "social label".

text.p: International Labour Organisation (ILO) chief Michel Hansenne proposed on Wednesday the creation of a "social label" for goods from countries which ensure key standards for their workers.

The suggestion, in a report for the United Nations agency's annual conference in June, was part of a three-step programme Hansenne argues could ensure social progress is not swept aside in the rush to a global economy and open trade.

The label, he said, "could be awarded to countries complying with a set of fundamental principles and (labour) rights and agreeing to have their practices supervised by an international inspection....which is reliable and legally independent."

The inspection system, the ILO Director-General added, could be set up under a voluntary convention which would allow each state "to decide freely whether to give an overall social label to all goods produced on its territory."

But to qualify, countries would have to accept the obligation to observe the core conventions of the ILO -- which has no sanctions mechanism -- covering freedom of association, forced and child labour, and non-discrimination.
"Ratification of such a Convention would be attractive in terms of real economic interests, and not only from a moral standpoint," he declared.

Hansenne's proposal was the latest turn in a long debate on how workers' rights can be best protected and exploitation prevented as national barriers to investment and trade crumble and firms look around the world to cut their labour costs.

Developing countries last year fought off a bid led by the United States and backed by European countries to have the so-called link between trade and labour brought onto the agenda of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

At its first Ministerial Meeting in Singapore in December, the WTO's now 130 members agreed the ILO was "the competent body to set and deal with" labour standards, effectively passing the ball back to the U.N.'s oldest agency.

U.S. officials, backed by worker organisations like the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), seek eventual enforcement of the ILO core standards through WTO trading rules.

This would make it possible to take any country seen as violating these standards to the WTO's dispute settlement system which can approve trade sanctions against members found by a neutral panel to be in breach.

Western officials insisted that some movement in this direction was vital to head off rising anger among workers in the richer countries who see globalisation as depriving them of jobs flowing to cheaper-labour economies.
But developing countries saw this argument as masking an effort to enshrine protection of Western goods through the WTO against competition from their own less-costly products.

Hansenne, a former Belgian minister of social affairs who is expected to step down next year, argued in Wednesday's report that social progress must go hand in hand with trade liberalisation in the globalising world economy.
Otherwise, he said, trade disputes and consumer boycotts will multiply, weakening political support for the globalisation process and open trade and leading to new protectionism.

Soon after the WTO's Singapore meeting, to which he was "disinvited" after pressure from some developing countries angered at his stance, he made clear he would be launching an effort to get more teeth for the 174-member agency.

In his report, he said the ILO would be pushing a campaign for all member countries to sign up to the core conventions, and for a change in the agency's Constitution to allow monitoring of all member states, whether they had signed up or not.
